entries.title: BITCOIN IMPLEMENTATION
entries.body:
Refers to software that applies and follows the rules defined by the Bitcoin protocol. What is called “Bitcoin” is generally the electronic cash system. It is a protocol that specifies rules. It is represented, concretely, by nodes that form a network. This system does not specifically have code. It is simply a set of major tacit rules imposed by the consensus of users through their nodes. On the other hand, what does have computer code, and can therefore be developed, maintained and modified, is rather the Bitcoin node software. These are independent implementations of the Bitcoin protocol, which can connect to the rest of the network.

Among Bitcoin implementations, Bitcoin Core is by far the most widespread, since it represents the vast majority of the node network. However, there are also minority implementations such as btcd, Bcoin, and Bitcoin Knots. Despite the diversity of software clients available, the predominance of Bitcoin Core on the network gives it an almost exclusive influence over the enforcement of the Bitcoin protocol. It is therefore said that Bitcoin Core in practice represents the Bitcoin protocol itself.

entries.title: I2P
entries.body:
Anonymous communication network designed to ensure the confidentiality of exchanges on the Internet. Like Tor, I2P encrypts network data and uses a routing system called *garlic routing*. This method guarantees the anonymity of communications by passing them through intermediary servers that redirect the information without knowing the identity of the sender or that of the recipient. Just like Tor, I2P can be used on a Bitcoin node, in order to secure its network communications.

*The acronym “I2P” stands for “Invisible Internet Project”.*

entries.title: IBD - INITIAL BLOCK DOWNLOAD
entries.body:
Refers to the process by which a node downloads and verifies the blockchain from the Genesis block, and synchronizes with the other nodes of the Bitcoin network. The IBD must be performed when launching a new full node. At the start of this initial synchronization, the node has no information about previous transactions. It therefore downloads each block from the other nodes of the network, verifies its validity, then adds it to its local version of the blockchain. It should be noted that the IBD can be long and resource-intensive because of the growing size of the blockchain and of the UTXO set. How quickly it completes depends on the computing power of the computer hosting the node, its RAM, the speed of the storage device, and the bandwidth. To give you an idea, if you have a fast internet connection and the node is hosted on the latest MacBook with plenty of RAM, the IBD will only take a few hours. On the other hand, if you use a single-board computer such as a Raspberry Pi, the IBD may take a week or more.

*In French, it is generally accepted to speak directly of an IBD.*

entries.title: IMMERSION COOLING
entries.body: Cooling technique used in mining, in which the ASICs are immersed in a non-conductive liquid to dissipate the heat they produce. Immersion has several advantages over air cooling. First of all, there is no need to use fans, which reduces energy consumption. Also, the machines are protected from dust, which improves their performance and longevity. Immersion also allows better heat dissipation, because the components are in direct contact with the cooling fluid.

entries.title: INBOUND CAPACITY
entries.body: Refers to the maximum amount of bitcoins that a node can receive through a specific channel on the Lightning Network. It depends on the funds that the peer node committed to the channel when it was opened, or that one has sent during an outgoing Lightning payment or a routing.

entries.title: INDEX - KEY
entries.body: In the context of an HD wallet, refers to the sequential number assigned to a child key generated from a parent key. This index is used in combination with the parent key and the parent chain code to deterministically derive unique child keys. It allows a structured organization and the reproducible generation of multiple sibling child key pairs from a single parent key. It is a 32-bit integer used in the derivation function `HMAC-SHA512`. This number therefore makes it possible to differentiate sibling child keys within an HD wallet.

entries.title: INDEXES/TXINDEX/
entries.body: Files in Bitcoin Core that are dedicated to indexing all the transactions present in the blockchain. This indexing makes it possible to quickly look up detailed information about a transaction using its identifier (TXID), without having to go through the entire blockchain. Creating these index files is an option that is not enabled by default in Bitcoin Core. If this feature is not enabled, your node will only index the transactions associated with the wallets attached to your node. To enable indexing of all transactions, you must set the `txindex=1` parameter in the `bitcoin.conf` file. This option is particularly useful for applications and services that frequently search the Bitcoin transaction history.

entries.title: INFLATION
entries.body:
Refers to the increase in the money supply in circulation, leading to a decline in the value of each unit of currency and a rise in the prices of goods and services. For state currencies, this phenomenon occurs when central banks issue new monetary units.

In the context of Bitcoin, inflation is controlled by the protocol. New bitcoins are generated with each block validation through the subsidy awarded to the winning miner. This subsidy was initially 50 BTC per block and it is halved every 210,000 blocks in an event known as the “halving”. The total issuance of bitcoins is capped at approximately 21 million units, which means that the monetary inflation of BTC is decreasing and will stop once the maximum number of units is reached.

entries.title: INPUT
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, an input within a transaction refers to the UTXOs (*Unspent Transaction Outputs*) used as source funds to satisfy the outputs. Each input contains references to previous UTXOs, which will then be consumed by the transaction. These inputs are used to fund new UTXOs that will be created as outputs of the transaction, and that can then be spent in future transactions. 

The role of a Bitcoin transaction is therefore to consume UTXOs as inputs, and to create new UTXOs as outputs. The difference between the two corresponds to the transaction fees, which can be collected by the miner who validates the block. 

From a broader point of view, in computing, the term “input” generally refers to the data provided to a function, an algorithm, or a system as operands or information required to perform an operation or a calculation. In this sense, the term is used more generically to describe anything provided to a process in order to obtain a result or an output. For example, when data is passed into a cryptographic hash function, this information is called an “input”.

entries.title: INSCRIPTIONS
entries.body:
In the context of Ordinal theory, inscriptions are arbitrary content engraved on sats, turning them into digital artifacts native to Bitcoin. Inscriptions are made through transactions that expose the content of the information in the script of a Taproot input in this way:

```text
OP_FALSE
OP_IF
  OP_PUSH "ord"
  OP_PUSH 1
  OP_PUSH "<content type>"
  OP_PUSH 0
  OP_PUSH "<la data ici>"
OP_ENDIF
```

These digital artifacts, like NFTs, can be traded and kept.

entries.title: INTERFACE
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Interface* refers to the set of instructions that decode the binary data compiled in a *Schema* or within the operations and states of a contract. It serves as an interpretation layer, in order to transform raw information into a representation readable by the user or their *wallet*.

entries.title: INTERFACE IMPLEMENTATION
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Interface Implementation* refers to the set of declarations establishing the correspondence between an *Interface* and a *Schema*. It makes it possible to carry out the semantic translation of a contract's binary data, in order to ensure its correct interpretation by the user or by applications, such as *wallets*.

entries.title: IOU
entries.body: Acronym of the English _I Owe You_ (in French “Je te dois”) used in the context of Bitcoin to refer to digital assets that are backed by underlying assets to which they should normally be pegged. This term applies in particular to *stablecoins* or to representations of BTC on systems external to Bitcoin, such as *sidechains*, *drivechains*, exchange platforms, or even ETFs. These digital assets represent a promise of value equivalent to that of the underlying asset.

entries.title: IP REPORT
entries.body: Button found on ASICs that makes it possible to quickly find the IP address of the machine on the local network. To use this feature, you must press the ASIC's *IP Report* button for a few seconds. Then, using specialized software on a computer connected to the same network, the miner's IP address will be displayed on the screen. This button notably makes it easy to locate a machine on the local network when you have several machines.

entries.title: IP_ASN.MAP
entries.body: File used in Bitcoin Core to store the ASMAP, which improves the *bucketing* (that is, the grouping) of IP addresses, based on autonomous system numbers (ASNs). Rather than grouping outbound connections by IP network prefixes (`/16`), this file makes it possible to diversify connections by establishing a map from IP addresses to ASNs, which are unique identifiers for each network on the Internet. The idea is to improve the security and topology of the Bitcoin network by diversifying connections to protect against certain attacks (notably the Erebus attack).

entries.title: ISSUE
entries.body: In the context of GitHub and other code hosting platforms, an issue is a report that flags a bug, proposes an improvement or suggests a new feature. It serves as a discussion point for contributors and makes it possible to track tasks to be accomplished or problems to be solved in the project. As a Bitcoin user, you can help the open source software you use by reporting possible bugs through issues on the project's repository.

entries.title: LIGHTNING INVOICE
entries.body:
Lightning payment request generated by the recipient, which contains all the information necessary to carry out the transaction.

A Lightning invoice contains the destination of the payment in the form of the public key of the recipient node, but also a prefix `ln`, the amount, a time before expiry, the hash of the secret used in the context of HTLCs, as well as other metadata, some of it optional, such as options relating to routing. These invoices are defined by the BOLT-11 standard. Once paid, a Lightning invoice can no longer be reused.

entries.title: RGB INVOICE
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, an *Invoice* takes the form of a URI prefixed by `rgb:`, which includes the information essential to the construction of a *State Transition* by the payer. In practice, it is an invoice that allows the counterparty to generate the appropriate transition to transfer an asset or update the state of a contract.
